newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel still awaits Netanyahu's economic reforms.
newsitem.headline: Israel still awaits Netanyahu's economic reforms.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has promised sweeping economic reforms but after seven months in office analysts note that he has yet to complete a single major initiative.
"Netanyahu clearly failed to deliver on election promises to carry out revolutionary economic measures immediately after assuming office," said Amotz Asa-El, economics editor of The Jerusalem Post.
The delays are in sharp contrast to Netanyahu's declarations before and after elections in May.

"Israel has had incremental reforms....It is not that nothing has been done. Quite a few things, important things, have been and we intend to do more, a lot more, in a compressed time," Netanyahu said shortly after taking office in June.

Since then, however, the government abandoned in mid-stream the Brodet committee proposals for reforming the capital markets, and has yet to finish deliberations on a Treasury plan to undertake structural reforms to enhance competition.

Other reforms have been promised but have yet to be formally unveiled. For example, officials have been promising since October that there will be a plan to revive the nearly moribund privatisation programme.
Plans to reform the tax system and further liberalise foreign currency regulations have been discussed but not formally proposed.

Treasury sources said the structural changes were on the agenda for Wednesday's cabinet meeting, and sources at the prime minister's office said the ministerial privatisation committee would meet on the privatisation programme later that day.
Both Netanyahu and his finance minister, Dan Meridor, see the reforms as crucial to return the economy to the high growth of the early 1990s.

Growth slowed to an estimated 4.4 percent last year from 7.1 percent in 1995, according to the Central Bureau of Statistics. The Treasury is expecting gross domestic product to grow four percent this year, although many private sector economists are expecting a slower rate.

Analysts said Netanyahu and Meridor are strong supporters of economic liberalisation. But Doron Tsur, head of research at Sahar Securities, said he doubted they had the full support of their Likud party rank and file or of their coalition partners.
"The difference between this government and the previous (Labour party) government are not great," he said.

"It isn't natural for a Likud voter to embrace (privatisation and deregulation) as it would be for a typical Tory voter," added Asa-El, who also blamed the delays on the inexperience of Netanyahu and his advisers, and their reluctance to take on political opposition.
Analysts say Meridor's effectiveness has been hurt by political infighting with officials in Netanyahu's office. They add that the prime minister's economic advisers do not have much influence.

Officials have said the privatisation plan calls for selling shares in Bezeq Israel Telecom, Zim Israel Navigation and Israel Chemicals Ltd. The 1997 budget forecasts revenues of about $1.3 billion from privatisation, compared with less than $200 million last year.

Despite delays, Tsur said he believes the government is fully committed to selling state-owned enterprises. The problem is the slump in the local stock market, which has made it virtually impossible to float shares for the last three years.
"It takes two to tango. The government wants to sell but you need demand. It's not that they don't want to sell," he said.

In fact, the government appears to be making progress in selling shares in the commercial banks. A secondary offering in Israel Discount Bank is expected to occur next month, and officials are weighing a global offering in Bank Leumi. Officials have said there is renewed interest by foreign investors in the controlling stakes in Bank Hapoalim and Bank Leumi.

Earlier this month, the cabinet approved 17 of 25 measures proposed by the Treasury to enhance competition. However, most of the changes, which include a grab-bag of items such as a limited opening of public transport to competition, need to be studied by committees first before they can be implemented.
Treasury sources said the tax reforms on the drawing board are aimed at reducing income tax rates and ending certain tax exemptions. Meridor has promised to unveil the proposal early this year.
